summary: Brian Vagg, a Northern California (Zone 9b) gardener, shares his plan to convert his back lawn into a food forest on a forum thread titled 'Lawn to Food Forest' on permies.com. The plan covers drip irrigation replacing sprinklers, hugelkultur swales filled with rotted wood, cardboard and 8-12 inches of compost over the lawn, bare-root fruit trees and berries with logs under each, and a legume cover crop under 4-6 inches of straw. Replies discuss keyhole hugel layout, nitrogen-fixing understory, animals, compost and straw contamination concerns, vines for the sunny wall, water harvesting with depressions, and soil concerns.
one_line: A Northern California gardener seeks feedback on converting a back lawn into a hugelkultur-based food forest with drip irrigation, compost, and bare-root trees.
key_facts: Brian Vagg is converting his back lawn to be part of his food forest and is in Northern California - Zone 9b.
Brian Vagg reports that his area gets anywhere from 5 - 6 months without rain.
Brian Vagg plans to convert his lawn sprinklers into a drip system.
Brian Vagg plans to dig trenches, fill them with old rotted wood and recover them with dirt to make hugelkulture swales.
Brian Vagg plans to cover the lawn with cardboard and about 8 - 12 inches of really finished compost.
Brian Vagg plans to seed a cover crop (mostly legumes) and then add a layer of 4 - 6 inches of straw.
Matt Saager suggested arranging hugel beds in an interlocking keyhole arrangement to maximize sun exposure.
Matt Saager suggested adding nitrogen-fixing trees or bushes as an understory, pruned short, to benefit the fruit trees long term.
Alder Burns advised that seeding a cover crop and mulching over it with 4-6 inches of straw will almost certainly smother the seedlings, saying 'cover crop or mulch, but not both at the same time.'
Alder Burns recommended starting with gardens and planting young trees and perennials among the vegetables to simulate succession.
Kris Minto suggested wood chips from a tree company as a mulch that holds moisture and is less likely to be sprayed than straw.
Brian Vagg's compost comes from the local landfill, which he used last year for his annual garden with good results.
Brian Vagg plans to get bare root trees in by January and has access to a good supply of horse manure.
Brian Vagg's chosen vines for the southwest-facing wall include kiwis and Akebia.
Andy Reed advised planting fruit trees in dug-out depressions at least the size of the drip line of the mature trees to harvest water.
Brian Vagg noted there is very little soil underneath the existing lawn and a french drain under the upper and lower walls.
